pr.title: Fit the passkeys plan to the store package
pr.head: c39d2eda8615b6e98c6a3c80df69fe1587c7eeaf

summary: multipass keeps its plans for future work under docs/projects. Three of them were merged together: the mergeable store, which lets two copies of the store combine entry by entry; the vault key, which turns the store into a package, a directory of encrypted files that are written once and never modified; and session unlock. The passkeys plan, which describes an iPhone and Mac app that signs you in with passkeys kept in the store, was written before the package existed. It still described one store.age file synced through iCloud Drive, with a conflict screen for when two devices saved at once.

This pull request fits the passkeys plan, still a draft, to the package. The extension now opens the package and saves a registration as a new file, and the iCloud container holds Documents/store.multipass. The conflict screen gives way to the merge, and the plan states the merge's limit: two offline changes to the same entry keep only the newer one. § 2.3 explains why the Keychain item keeps the passphrase rather than the vault key, and what the extension does when key files under an old and a new passphrase are both present after passwd. The plan also decides how a new passkey's entry is named (questions 7 to 9), and the app declares .multipass as a package type.

Small edits to three neighboring plans follow from that. The vault-key plan says plainly when a passphrase prompt compacts and which steps a save follows, the session-unlock plan records the passkeys plan's choice to keep the passphrase in the Keychain, and the shared-vaults plan names the passkeys plan's CryptoKit exemption in full.
The latest review found the head clean. Nothing in this pull request is code, and nothing is built yet.

cards.title: Terms
cards.html:
• Package: the store as a directory, store.multipass, of age-encrypted files that are never modified once written.
  • Key file: key.<gen>.age, encrypted under your passphrase, holding the random vault key and the keys it replaced.
  • Store file: store.<gen>.<random>.age, a whole store encrypted under the vault key's text. Each save writes a new one.
  • Merge: opening decrypts every store file and keeps, for each entry, the version with the newest modified stamp.
  • Rotation: replacing the vault key, at a prompt when the key is 14 or more days old and on every passwd.

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html:
• Four rounds of review found five problems: the same-entry merge loss, no rule for key files under two passphrases, passages that still described one file, a read-only sign-in that could fail, and a dropped sentence that the session-unlock plan cites. All five are fixed at this head.
  • The latest review suggests that the prototype check how iCloud Drive syncs a folder once the app declares it a package.
  • Still owed as a follow-up: how a store reaches the iCloud container.
  • The passkeys plan stays draft, with only question 5 open, so readiness does not gate the review.

groups.title: The passkeys plan on the store package
groups.kicker: How the app's extension opens, saves, unlocks, and syncs the store now that it is a package
intro: The passkeys app's AutoFill extension is what macOS and iOS call when a site asks for a passkey. It unlocks the store, signs with a passkey from it, and, for a new passkey, saves one. Before this change the plan had it decrypt and replace a single file, and refuse to save while iCloud held two versions of that file.

With the vault-key package, a save adds a new store file and deletes only the files it read, so iCloud never holds two versions of one file. The plan now relies on the merge instead of a conflict screen. Changes to different entries both survive. Changes to the same entry keep only the newer one, and because a new passkey joins the site's existing entry (question 7), two offline registrations for one site, or a registration beside a password edit, lose one change without a warning. § 2.4 states that limit, and § 4 records it.

The Keychain item still holds the passphrase. The vault key changes at least every 21 days and on every passwd, so an item holding it would go stale, and only the passphrase can encrypt the new key file a rotation writes. After passwd, the package can briefly hold key files under both the old and the new passphrase. § 2.3 now says the extension neither signs nor saves while any key file does not open with the item's passphrase. It asks for the other passphrase, as the vault-key plan's prompt does, and fails with multipass needs your other passphrase when you cancel, so it never signs from an older lineage's store. The CLI never reads or writes the item.

checks.text: The merge works entry by entry: when two devices change the same entry, the newer version wins and the older change is dropped. The plan accepts that limit rather than preventing it.

files.note: § 2, § 2.1, § 2.3, § 2.4, § 2.5, § 4, § 5, and § 6 now describe the package, the merge and its limit, the passphrase in the Keychain, the decided entry names, and the package-type declaration.

checks.text: A cancelled other-passphrase field fails both a sign-in and a registration, whatever iCloud has deleted, and the § 4 row at line 116 expects that. The paragraph again ends with the CLI sentence that the session-unlock plan cites. Checked against the vault-key plan's § 2.3 steps 3 and 4, § 2.5's deletion order, and session-unlock § 2.10 at this head.

The item's access control (biometryCurrentSet) and accessibility (whenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly) are unchanged. Checked against the vault-key plan's § 2.5 and § 2.8: passwd rotates and deletes the old key file, so once that deletion syncs, an old passphrase in the item opens nothing in the package.
The same-entry limit matches the mergeable-store plan's § 2.3, which keeps the version with the largest modified. Checked by reading that section, and the § 4 rows at lines 114 and 115, at this head.

The app now declares .multipass as a package type, as the vault-key plan's § 2.1 expects. iCloud Drive may then treat the folder as one document, so the review suggests the prototype check that it still syncs the files inside one by one.
The recovery row runs the vault-key plan's § 2.7 steps: the key file first, then the store file with the key's text. Checked against § 2.7 at this head.

groups.title: Edits to the neighboring plans
groups.kicker: Small edits that keep the vault-key, session-unlock, and shared-vaults plans in step
intro: At a passphrase prompt, opening the package can end with one of two clean-ups. A rotation writes a new key file and one merged store file under the new key. A compaction, when there was no rotation, writes one merged store file under the current key. Both delete the files they read. The vault-key plan's step 7 used to begin "Otherwise", which, after a step about the move record, read as "compact only when there is no move record". It now says "When it did not rotate". Its § 2.4 now points a save at steps 4 and 7, the merge and the compaction, rather than at step 6, the move-record check that session unlock's agent never runs.

The session-unlock plan's § 2.10 said the passkeys extension could keep the vault key in its Keychain item, and left the choice to the passkeys plan. It now records the choice, the passphrase, and the reason. Its § 2.11 names to_text(cutoff) as the mergeable-store plan defines it.
The shared-vaults plan, merged from main into this branch, now names both parts of the passkeys plan's CryptoKit exemption: the P-256 calls and the session-unlock enclave calls.

files.note: § 2.3 step 7 names rotation as the condition for compacting, and § 2.4 step 1 cites the right steps.

checks.text: Matches § 2.5, whose step 2 already writes one merged store file during a rotation, and step 3's read-only open still forbids compaction. No test in § 4 depends on the old wording. Checked by reading § 2.3 to § 2.6 and § 4 at this head.

files.note: § 2.10 says the passkeys extension keeps the passphrase, not the vault key, and why; § 2.11 names to_text(cutoff).
The AGENTS.md row names the whole passkeys exemption, the P-256 calls and the enclave calls.
